title: Rainy Season Hiking Gear: 10 Essential Picks to Stay Dry
meta_title: Rainy Season Hiking Gear: 10 Essential Picks to Stay Dry
meta_description: Rainy season hiking gear for Kenya's short rains: jackets, rain pants, boots, gaiters and dry bags that keep you safe and comfortable.
excerpt: The short rains are here. This guide to rainy season hiking gear covers the waterproof layers, footwear and small extras that keep Kenyan hikers dry and safe.
content:
Rainy season hiking gear is the difference between a wet, miserable slog and a day on the trail you actually enjoy when the clouds open. With Kenya's short rains arriving, now is the time to check that your jacket still keeps water out, your boots still grip and your pack has a plan for the downpour.

Plenty of Kenyan hikers simply stop hiking between October and December, and miss out on green hills, quieter trails and cool walking weather. This guide to rainy season hiking gear walks you through the 10 pieces of kit that matter most, how to layer them, and the habits that keep you safe on slippery ground, so you can keep hiking right through the wet months.

Key Takeaways

  • Seasons: Kenya's long rains usually run from about March to May, and the short rains from about October to December.
  • This year: the Kenya Meteorological Service Authority's outlook points to wetter-than-normal short rains over much of the country in 2026.
  • Core rainy season hiking gear: a waterproof jacket, rain pants, grippy boots, gaiters and a way to keep your pack contents dry.
  • Skip cotton: it holds water and chills you fast; choose wool or synthetic layers.
  • Stay dry early: put rain gear on before you get wet, not after.

Why Rainy Season Hiking Gear Matters in Kenya

Rain on a Kenyan trail is rarely a gentle drizzle. Afternoon storms on the Aberdares, Mt Kenya or the Ngong Hills can bring heavy downpours, sudden wind and a sharp drop in temperature within minutes. At altitude, being soaked through and cold is not just uncomfortable; it can lead to hypothermia, even close to the equator.

The trails change too. Red soil turns to slick mud, volcanic ash becomes greasy, and streams can rise quickly after a storm. The right rainy season hiking gear keeps your core warm, your feet stable and your essentials dry, which means you can make good decisions instead of rushing back to the car.

For 2026, the Kenya Meteorological Service Authority (KMSA) expects enhanced rainfall over around 80% of the country during the October to December season, with onset forecast for the second and third weeks of October in most areas, as reported by The Star. That makes it a good year to get your rainy season hiking gear sorted early.

10 Essential Pieces of Rainy Season Hiking Gear

You do not need to buy all your rainy season hiking gear at once. Start with the items at the top of this list, which protect you most, and add the rest as you go. All of our kit is quality thrifted gear, carefully checked so that proper waterproof equipment costs a fraction of the new price.

1. A waterproof, breathable rain jacket

This is the heart of your rainy season hiking gear. Look for a jacket with taped seams, a hood with an adjustable peak that you can tighten around your face, and pit zips or a front zip that lets heat out on climbs. A breathable membrane helps sweat escape, so you stay drier on the inside as well as the outside. Browse our rain jackets for tested options.

2. Waterproof rain pants

Rain pants are the most overlooked rainy season hiking gear. Wet trousers stick to your legs, rub, and pull heat from your body for hours. A pair of Waterproof Rain Pants pulls on over your hiking trousers when the rain starts. Choose a pair with ankle zips so you can get them on and off without removing your boots.

3. Hiking boots with deep tread

Mud and wet rock call for real grip, so boots are core rainy season hiking gear. Waterproof boots with deep, widely spaced lugs shed mud better and keep your feet drier in long grass and puddles. Ankle support also helps on slippery descents, which is where most rainy season falls happen.

4. Gaiters

Gaiters seal the gap between your boots and your trousers, stopping mud, water and grit from running into your boots. Our Waterproof Leg Gaiters are a simple upgrade that make a big difference in wet grass, bamboo zones and boggy moorland.

5. Wool socks, plus a spare pair

Merino wool socks keep feet warmer than cotton even when damp, and they resist odour on long days. Always pack one dry spare pair in a sealed bag. Changing into dry socks at lunch is one of the cheapest comfort upgrades on any wet hike, and it helps prevent blisters.

6. Quick-dry base layers

Your base layer sits against your skin, so it should move sweat away and dry fast. Synthetic or merino tops work well; cotton T-shirts do the opposite, staying wet and cold. A long-sleeve quick-dry top is a versatile choice for most Kenyan trails.

7. A warm mid layer

When you stop for a break in the rain, your body cools quickly. A fleece or synthetic insulated jacket keeps its warmth better than down when damp, which makes it the safer choice for wet days. Keep it in a dry bag and put it on the moment you stop.

8. Waterproof gloves

Cold, wet hands make it hard to open zips, use trekking poles or eat. Insulated waterproof gloves such as our Thinsulate Waterproof Hiking Gloves are well worth carrying on higher hikes such as the Aberdares and Mt Kenya, where rain at altitude can feel wintry.

9. Pack cover and dry bags

Most backpacks are not fully waterproof, even if the fabric looks tough. Use a pack rain cover on the outside and dry bags, or sturdy plastic bags, on the inside for your warm layer, spare socks, phone and first-aid kit. Protecting your other rainy season hiking gear inside the pack is just as important as wearing it. Pack the things you need most near the top so you are not unpacking in a downpour.

10. A reliable headlamp

Storms slow you down, and dark clouds make late afternoons gloomy. A water-resistant headlamp, such as our Waterproof Rechargeable Headlamp, means a delayed descent never leaves you stuck in the dark. Charge it the night before every hike.

How to Layer Your Rainy Season Hiking Gear

Layering your rainy season hiking gear lets you adjust to changing conditions without getting soaked from the outside or from your own sweat. Think of it as three jobs: move moisture, hold warmth and block weather.

Start light

Begin the hike in a quick-dry base layer and light trousers, even if it is cool at the trailhead. You will warm up within minutes of climbing, and starting too warm means sweating into your layers before the rain even arrives.

Shell up early

Put your rain jacket and rain pants on at the first steady drops, not when you are already damp. It is much easier to stay dry than to dry out once you are wet. Open the vents on climbs, then close them on exposed ridges.

Add warmth when you stop

Your fleece or insulated jacket goes on at every break, under or over your shell depending on the rain. Take it off again before you start walking, so it stays dry for the next stop.

Caring for Your Rainy Season Hiking Gear

Good rainy season hiking gear lasts for years if you look after it. After a wet hike, rinse mud off boots and gaiters with clean water, stuff boots with newspaper and let everything dry slowly in the shade, away from direct heat that can crack leather and damage glue.

Rain jackets and pants work best when clean. Dirt, sweat and sunscreen clog the fabric, so wash them occasionally with a technical cleaner rather than ordinary detergent. If water stops beading on the surface, the outer coating has worn and can be refreshed with a wash-in or spray-on reproofer.

Store all your rainy season hiking gear clean and fully dry. Folding a damp jacket into a bag for weeks is the fastest way to ruin the waterproof coating and invite mould.

Wet-Weather Packing Checklist

  • Waterproof jacket with a good hood
  • Rain pants with ankle zips
  • Boots with deep tread, plus gaiters
  • Wool socks and one dry spare pair in a sealed bag
  • Quick-dry base layer and a fleece or synthetic mid layer
  • Waterproof gloves and a warm hat for high-altitude hikes
  • Pack cover and dry bags for your essentials
  • Charged headlamp, snacks, water and a small first-aid kit
  • Phone in a waterproof pouch or zip-lock bag

Staying Safe on Wet Trails

Rainy season hiking gear is only half the story. The way you hike in the rain matters just as much. These habits, many of which are echoed in REI's guide to hiking in the rain, will help you get home safely.

Check the forecast and start early

In Kenya, rain often builds through the afternoon. Starting early gives you the best chance of finishing exposed sections before storms arrive. Check the latest forecast the night before and the morning of your hike, and have a shorter backup route in mind.

Respect rivers and gullies

Streams can rise fast after heavy rain upstream. Never cross fast-flowing water above knee height, and if a crossing looks doubtful, wait or turn back. Unclip your backpack hip belt before crossing so you can slip out of it if you fall.

Get off high ground in storms

If you hear thunder, move off exposed summits and ridges as quickly and safely as you can. Avoid sheltering under isolated trees.

Watch for signs of cold

Uncontrolled shivering, clumsiness, slurred speech and confusion are warning signs of hypothermia. Stop, get into dry layers, eat something and warm up. Keep an eye on everyone in your group, because people often do not notice it in themselves.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the most important rainy season hiking gear to buy first?

Start with a properly waterproof jacket and boots with good grip. Together they protect your core warmth and your footing, which are the two things most likely to cause trouble on a wet hike. Rain pants and gaiters are the next priorities.

Is a poncho good enough as rainy season hiking gear?

A poncho is cheap and covers your backpack too, which makes it useful on lower, sheltered trails. On windy ridges and higher mountains it can flap about and let rain in, so a fitted rain jacket is the better choice there.

Is it safe to hike in Kenya during the short rains?

Many trails are fine with the right preparation. Start early, check the forecast, avoid river crossings after heavy rain and turn back if storms build. Some routes become very muddy, so choose trails that suit your experience.

Can thrifted waterproof gear still keep me dry?

Yes. Quality rainy season hiking gear is built to last, and a well-cared-for pre-owned jacket or pair of boots can perform just as well as new. We check our gear before it goes on sale, and a reproofing treatment can refresh the outer coating if it has worn.

Should I hike in shorts during the rains?

On warm, low-altitude trails some hikers prefer shorts, because wet legs dry faster than wet trousers. At higher altitudes, or when it is windy, cover up with rain pants to stay warm.

Final Thoughts

The short rains do not have to put your hiking on hold. With the right rainy season hiking gear, a little planning and sensible habits on the trail, wet months bring green landscapes, quiet paths and cool air. Check your jacket, boots and dry bags this week, fill the gaps, and get back out there.
